source.spoken_script: Two criminals died beside Jesus that afternoon. Same nails. Same hill. Same distance. Opposite eternities. Both guilty. Both just as close. Both spoke. If thou be Christ, save thyself and us. A taunt, not a prayer. The other thief rebuked him. And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss. A confession. A verdict: innocent. Then one request. Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise. He asked for someday. Jesus gave him that same afternoon. No merit. Just repentance and trust. We are all one of those two men. Ask what the thief asked. Remember me. Then hear his answer. With me. Today. Paradise.

platforms.title: The Thief on the Cross: Same Nails, Opposite Eternities
platforms.description:
Two criminals were crucified beside Jesus on the same afternoon. Same sentence, same nails, same hill, the same few feet from the Savior. And they went to opposite eternities.

Both were guilty, and both said so. One turned his guilt into a taunt: if thou be Christ, save thyself and us. The other turned his into a confession: "we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss." A dying criminal delivered the trial verdict Jerusalem refused to give: innocent.

Then the request that has carried hope to deathbeds ever since: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. He asked for a someday. The answer outran the request:

"And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43, KJV).

In this piece: the two thieves in Luke's own words, why the penitent thief's confession matters as much as his request, and what this scene settles about salvation: no merit, no ritual, no time left to earn anything. Repentance and trust, answered the same afternoon, guaranteed by Christ's own Verily.

We are all one of those two men. Ask what the thief asked. Then hear the answer: with me. Today. Paradise.
